name: Liam Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I push dirt. I run a D11 dozer at the Westfield coal mine near Harlow, mostly ripping and pushing overburden, the rock on top of the coal, so the excavators can get at it. Twelve-hour shifts, seven on, seven off. I like it because nobody bothers you in a dozer, it's just you and the blade. What wears me out is the night shifts and the rattle, my back's already complaining at twenty-seven.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's home like, and how do you feel about the mine's future?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my girlfriend Amara, she rents a chair at a hair salon on Main Street. We've got about two months of bills saved, less since I bought the new truck. The company says the mine runs till 2038, but everyone knows coal's on the way out, so you hear a new closure rumour every few months. I try not to listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say told you so, it was all talk. At work we'd have a laugh about it. I don't do online, so that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, nothing changes, but nothing changing isn't great either, because coal's still dying on its own. The mine might close early whatever AI does. So I'm not exactly relaxed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep running the dozer and keep my head down. I'd try to put away 300 a month, which is hard with the truck payments. I'd maybe get my ticket for a grader too, so I've got more than one machine on my card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not about robots, about coal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the closure rumour turned out to be true?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Go to the quarry at Stonebridge or a road crew, they always need dozer operators. Less money, maybe a third less. Coal will close before any robot takes my dozer, so the thing I actually watch is the price of coal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Amara worry about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Amara's more worried than me, she reads the news. Her chair at the salon is steady, people always need haircuts. She says we should save more and I say we will, after the truck's paid off.

say: I'd say it was **all talk**, and we'd have a laugh at work.
I'd post **nothing** online, because that's just not something I do.
think: Coal is **dying on its own**, whatever AI does.
The mine might **close early**, so nothing changing still isn't great.
do: Keep running the **D11 dozer** and keep my head down.
Try to save **300 a month** around the truck payments.
Get a **grader ticket** so I can run more than one machine.
S0.quote: Coal will close before any robot takes my dozer, so the thing I actually watch is the price of coal.
fieldNote: His real worry is **coal closing**, which AI hype doesn't change.
He puts **truck payments** ahead of saving, even though his partner pushes.
His fallback is a **quarry or road crew**, at about a third less pay.

steps.text: Keep running the D11 dozer on seven-on, seven-off
Save 300 a month around the truck payments
Get a grader ticket to run a second machine

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office lot should be worried, not us. At lunch I'd say a robot can't feel when the ground's soft. That's about all I'd say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I know they've already trialled remote dozers at other coal mines, and the company talked about one here for 2027. If AI is speeding everything up, that trial goes ahead, and then it's two or three dozers run from a screen in town. That's less of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the grader ticket this year, and maybe the excavator one, so I'm useful on more machines. I'd cut back, no new gear for the truck, and get the savings up to three months. I'd not go near the remote dozer course though, sitting at a screen all day isn't for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, if I'm honest. It's two worries now, coal and the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not the remote dozer course, if that's where the jobs go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've seen it, it's a gaming chair and three screens in a portable building. I'd go mad. I'd rather push dirt in a quarry for less money than sit in a portable building steering a dozer I can't feel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said less money. What gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fishing trips with my brother, they're about 400 a go. Then eating out. Amara's already cut her gym.

say: I'd say the **office workers** should worry, not us.
I'd say a robot can't **feel soft ground** under the blade.
think: Other coal mines already trial **remote dozers**, and ours planned one.
If the trial goes ahead, fewer of us run **dozers from town**.
do: Get **grader and excavator** tickets this year.
Cut back on spending to lift savings to **three months**.
Stay away from the **remote dozer course** entirely.
feel: **Anxious**, with two worries now: **coal and machines**.
S1.quote: I'd rather push dirt in a quarry for less money than sit in a portable building steering a dozer I can't feel.
fieldNote: He'd take **less pay** in a quarry rather than move to a screen.
Spreading his **machine tickets** is his main defence.
He talks about cuts in **concrete terms**: fishing trips and eating out.

steps.text: Get grader and excavator tickets this year
Drop the 400-a-trip fishing weekends with my brother
Build savings up to three months of bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say someone needs to slow this down, the government or whoever. I'd say it at the pub. I don't think I'd say much more than that, because I don't know what the answer is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it scares me. Thinking AI by 2028 means the planners and the office go first, and then by 2031 the robot dozers are as good as me. I'd be thirty-one with a dozer ticket and two months of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, sell the truck and buy something cheap, which frees up about 600 a month. I'd start going to the union meetings I usually skip. I'd ask around at Stonebridge quarry and the road crews in the first year, because smaller outfits will be slower to buy robots. And I'd talk to Amara about moving in with her mum for a bit to save rent if it gets bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My gut drops thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only 2 years of warning change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's no time to wait, and waiting is what I'm good at. With ten years I'd sit tight, with two I'd have to jump. Selling my truck would hurt, because that truck is the first proper thing I ever bought with my own wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would smaller outfits be safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big companies buy robots first, because they've got the money. A quarry with four machines and an old owner is going to keep people longer. That's my guess anyway, I don't really know.

say: I'd say the **government** or someone needs to **slow this down**.
I'd admit I **don't know** what the answer is.
think: Thinking AI takes the **office** in 2028, then robot dozers match me by **2031**.
I'd be thirty-one with a **dozer ticket** and two months of savings.
do: Sell the **truck** and buy something cheap, freeing about **600 a month**.
Ask at **Stonebridge quarry** and road crews in the first year.
Start going to the **union meetings** I usually skip.
S2.quote: Selling my truck would hurt, because that truck is the first proper thing I ever bought with my own wages.
fieldNote: Two years forces him to **jump**, against his habit of waiting.
He bets **small outfits** will keep people longer, but admits it's a guess.
Moving in with his **partner's mother** is his fallback for rent.

steps.text: Sell the truck and buy a cheap car
Ask about jobs at Stonebridge quarry and road crews
Start going to union meetings at the mine
Move in with Amara's mum if rent gets too much

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is quick, but we can sort something out if people stay sensible. I'd say retrain people for the trades that last. I'm not one for big speeches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I know myself, I'd wait till about year four. By 2034 the robot dozers are here, and coal's probably near closing too. I'd need to be out of coal by about 2032 to be safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the grader and excavator tickets this year, and start saving 400 a month by cutting the fishing trips. Around 2029 I'd try for a job with the council road crew, which is steadier and slower to change. I'd keep the truck though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but there's time. It's like knowing a storm is coming next week, not tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait till year four. What would make you go sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Amara, probably, she'd keep at me. My girlfriend says I only change when the shed's already on fire, and she's not wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the gap between thinking AI and the robots mean for your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job's almost all hands-on, so the thinking AI doesn't take my seat. It takes the planners who tell me where to push. The robots are the ones that come for me, so I've got those three extra years.

say: I'd say **five years** is quick, but we can sort it out sensibly.
I'd say retrain people for **trades that last**.
think: I'd probably **wait till year four**, knowing myself.
I need to be **out of coal** by about 2032 to be safe.
do: Get **grader and excavator** tickets this year.
Save **400 a month** by cutting the fishing trips.
Apply to the **council road crew** around 2029.
feel: **Anxious**, but there's **time**, like a storm next week.
S3.quote: My girlfriend says I only change when the shed's already on fire, and she's not wrong.
fieldNote: He's honest that he'd **delay**, and that his girlfriend pushes him.
He sees the **three-year robot gap** as his real window.
A **council road crew** looks steadier to him than any mine.

steps.text: Get grader and excavator tickets this year
Cut the fishing trips to save 400 a month
Apply to the council road crew around 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years, plenty of time, no need to panic. I'd say that at work and I'd mean it, mostly. The young apprentices would roll their eyes at me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd probably do nothing for five years. Coal might close by 2038 anyway, so the robots by 2039 almost don't matter, coal gets me first. I'd need a plan for coal, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep dozing and pay off the truck first. Then from about 2028 I'd start saving properly, 400 a month. I'd get the grader ticket at some point and move to roads or a quarry before coal shuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it's the same uneasy I've had for years about coal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about leaving Harlow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, Amara's family is here and her chair at the salon has regulars. My town has a coal mine, a quarry and a road crew, and I'd rather work my way down that list than leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Amara change any plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We talked about getting married in a couple of years. In this one we'd still do it, maybe a small one. No point waiting ten years for robots.

say: I'd say **ten years** is plenty of time and **no need** to panic.
I'd mostly mean it, while the **young apprentices** roll their eyes.
think: I'd probably **do nothing** for the first five years.
**Coal closing** by 2038 gets me before the robots in 2039.
do: Keep dozing and **pay off the truck** first.
Get a **grader ticket** and move to roads before coal shuts.
feel: **Uneasy**, the same way I've felt about **coal** for years.
S4.quote: My town has a coal mine, a quarry and a road crew, and I'd rather work my way down that list than leave.
fieldNote: With ten years, robots matter less to him than **coal's end**.
He won't **leave town**, because his partner's family and clients are there.
He'd still plan a **small wedding** in a couple of years.

steps.text: Keep running the dozer at Westfield as normal
Pay off the truck, then save 400 a month
Move to a road crew or quarry before coal shuts
Wait a few years before making any big change

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it all lands at once, coal, robots, everything, and I'd only have two months saved. What would help is the company telling us straight what the plan is, and paying for tickets on new machines. And someone keeping smaller outfits going so there's somewhere to go.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about bodies. Twelve hours in a rattling dozer has already wrecked my back at twenty-seven, and nobody counts that when they say robots are taking our jobs.

headlineQuote: Twelve hours in a rattling dozer has already wrecked my back at twenty-seven, and nobody counts that when they say robots are taking our jobs.
portrait: Liam, 27, runs a **D11 dozer** at the Westfield coal mine near Harlow.
He lives with Amara, a hairdresser, and has only about **two months** saved.
He's **practical and quiet**, avoids AI tools and prefers to wait.
His long-running worry is **coal closing**, which shapes every scenario.
The **two-year warning** forces him to act, and that alarms him most.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it lands on top of coal's decline.
whatWouldHelp: A **straight plan** from the company and **paid tickets** for new machines.
